headline: US real estate debt attractive: proved resilient through 10%+ commercial property bear market in 2022–2024 due to disciplined structuring and portfolio diversification
reasoning: The US commercial real estate market experienced valuations falling 10% or more from 2022 to 2024, yet real estate debt portfolios withstood this because debt was structured correctly and portfolios were diversified. This demonstrates the asset class can offer good yields backed by stabilised real estate assets in a large, sophisticated market. The contrast with Australia — where a similar property value decline is raising concerns about debt resilience — underscores the quality differential.
quote: In the US market, commercial real estate had a basically a bear market in 2022 to sort of 2024. Valuations were off 10% or more, but that didn't mean real estate debt suffered. If debt is structured the right way and portfolios are diversified. A debt portfolio can withstand those kind of markets. The Australian market now is going through a similar thing where the real estate market is coming off. Now, if real estate debt has been done in a thoughtful and disciplined way, it should be able to weather that. But the fact that people are concerned that it may not reflect that there might be a couple of cracks or a couple of issues in the way that real estate debt here is done.

headline: European private credit an attractive opportunity driven by a large 2020–2021 corporate debt refinancing wave and undersupply of private credit capital in parts of the market
reasoning: A significant volume of European corporate debt was issued in 2020 and 2021 at low interest rates and is now maturing over the coming years, creating a refinancing cycle. In parts of the European credit market there is an undersupply of private credit capital, which is creating favourable conditions for lenders. This combination of high refinancing demand and limited supply of credit positions Europe as a compelling opportunity for private credit managers currently.

quote: Private credit is still a great asset class. It offers good yields with low volatility often double digit yields. headline: US private credit preferred: deep market post-GFC bank withdrawal enables true selectivity, diversification, and strong transparency via mandatory reporting
reasoning: Following the GFC, US banks largely withdrew from corporate lending, making private credit the primary source of corporate capital and creating a very large opportunity set. This depth allows managers to be selective with borrowers and build diversified sector portfolios. Mandatory reporting and extensive data collection offshore also provide much greater transparency than is available in Australia. These three factors — disciplined lending, diversification, and transparency — make the US market significantly more sophisticated.
quote: The US and European markets are much deeper and larger than the Australian market, so managers can be selective with who they're lending to, and they can have a diversified portfolio across sectors. And one reason for that is, I mean, in the US in particular, banks largely withdrew from corporate lending following the GFC. So private credit became a key source of capital for corporate lending, and it made the opportunity set very large. In Australia, banks still account for most business lending, so the opportunity set for private credit managers is not as big, and they can't be selective about who they're lending to, and they can't build portfolios that are as diversified.
